name: Working from home
research_question: How do people experience working from home since the pandemic?
reflexivity: I am a white British woman in my forties and a lecturer in organisational psychology. I have worked mostly from home since March 2020, at a desk in the spare room of a terraced house I share with my partner, and I chose to stay there when my university reopened. In that I am partly an insider: I know the green dot, the email answered at nine at night and the walk round the block before starting. I am an outsider in other ways. I care for no child or parent, my job is salaried and secure, and I have never had to learn a job through a screen, as Toby did, or to keep freelance clients, as Ffion does. I came to the topic because the pandemic made an arrangement that had belonged to a few people ordinary for millions almost overnight, while public talk about it stayed with productivity and office space rather than with what it is like to live with. I expected to hear about loneliness and the lost commute, since those were my own experience. I kept a short reflexive note after each interview and through coding, and the notes showed me warming most to the accounts nearest mine and being slow to take seriously the pleasure Ros and Glen find at home, so I went back to their interviews and coded them again. My own household is a simple one, which may have made me quick to notice who gets the quiet room in other people's; I have tried to show where that pattern comes from their words and not from mine.

Kemi.label: Both at once
Kemi.portrait: Kemi is an HR adviser for a supermarket chain's head office, at home full time since her office closed in 2020. She lives in a semi-detached house with her husband, Lewis, who works from the spare room, and their two children, seven and four. She works at the kitchen table and does both school runs. She is warm and quick, honest about mixed feelings, and laughs at herself before anyone else can.

Toby.label: The lad in the bedroom
Toby.portrait: Toby is a digital marketing executive at an agency, who started his job from his bedroom in 2021 and has rarely worked anywhere else. He is twenty-seven and lives in a shared house with three others, one a nurse on nights, and works at a small desk beside his bed. He is self-deprecating and funny, a little lost, and reluctant about home working he never chose.

Ros.label: The depot
Ros.portrait: Ros has worked in a council's revenues and benefits team for twenty-two years and now works at home three days a week. She lives in a semi-detached house with her son, seventeen, and her mother, eighty-three, lives alone ten minutes away. She is brisk, warm and plain-spoken, a keen home worker who would fight to keep it.

Glen.label: The man behind the door
Glen.portrait: Glen is sixty-three and a motor claims handler for an insurer, at home full time by his own request since the office reopened. He lives with his wife, Maureen, who retired two years before him, and works in their grown-up daughter's old box room. He is steady, orderly and gently humorous, and glad to be out of the open-plan office.

Dev.label: Dev from testing
Dev.portrait: Dev is thirty-four and a software tester for a bank that gave up most of its office after 2020. He lives with his partner, Sam, a dental nurse who goes out to work, in a one-bedroom flat where the kitchen table is his desk. He is thoughtful and candid, once keen on home working and now unsure, and finds it easier to be funny about it than to say it outright.

Ffion.label: The box in the hall
Ffion.portrait: Ffion is a freelance Welsh and English translator who has worked from home since her daughter was born in 2012. She lives with her daughter, now fourteen, in a two-bedroom ground-floor flat, and looks in on her father, who has early dementia and lives alone. She is precise and dry, proud of a craft she had to learn, and of keeping work in its corner.
